reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
clinicalPearls: Arises from an intrinsic developmental or functional abnormality of the lymphatic conducting vessels or nodes, not from an identifiable external insult, distinguishing it from secondary lymphoedema.
Classified by age of onset: congenital (present at or shortly after birth, includes Milroy disease), praecox (onset before 35 years, includes Meige disease) and tarda (onset after 35 years).
A positive Stemmer sign, the inability to pinch and tent a skin fold at the base of the second toe, is a reliable bedside indicator and is rarely falsely positive.
Swelling typically begins distally at the ankle or dorsum of the foot and ascends, is initially pitting and soft, then becomes non-pitting with dermal thickening, hyperkeratosis and peau d'orange.
Recurrent cellulitis is both a consequence and an accelerant of disease, each episode causing further lymphatic destruction and worsening oedema.
Several Mendelian forms exist, including FLT4 (VEGFR3) mutations in Milroy disease and FOXC2 mutations in lymphoedema-distichiasis, so a syndromic and family history is essential.
Lymphoscintigraphy is the standard confirmatory investigation, demonstrating delayed or absent tracer transport, dermal backflow and abnormal or absent nodes.
Chronic longstanding disease carries a small but important risk of cutaneous angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves phenomenon), warranting vigilance for new violaceous lesions.
reference.pathophysiology: Primary lymphoedema results from a constitutional abnormality of lymphatic development or function, which may take the form of aplasia, hypoplasia, hyperplasia with valvular incompetence, or lymph node fibrosis. Impaired lymphatic transport allows protein-rich interstitial fluid to accumulate, and the persistent high-protein oedema drives chronic low-grade inflammation, fibroblast activation, adipose deposition and progressive dermal and subcutaneous fibrosis. This creates a self-perpetuating cycle in which tissue remodelling further compromises the remaining lymphatics and predisposes to recurrent bacterial infection, which in turn accelerates lymphatic obliteration. A growing number of causative germline mutations affecting lymphangiogenesis pathways (for example VEGFR3/FLT4, FOXC2, SOX18, GJC2 and CCBE1) have been identified, explaining the hereditary and syndromic patterns.
additionalDifferentials: chronic venous insufficiency with venous oedema
systemic oedema from cardiac, renal or hepatic failure
secondary lymphoedema from malignancy, surgery, radiotherapy or filariasis
deep vein thrombosis and post-thrombotic syndrome
chronic regional pain syndrome with limb swelling
additionalInvestigations: venous duplex ultrasonography to exclude venous disease
MR or CT lymphangiography for anatomical mapping
targeted genetic testing and pedigree analysis in early-onset or syndromic cases
thyroid function and renal, hepatic and cardiac assessment to exclude systemic oedema
redFlags: rapidly progressive or markedly asymmetrical swelling raising concern for underlying malignancy
new violaceous or haemorrhagic cutaneous nodules suggesting angiosarcoma
unilateral limb swelling of recent onset in an older adult, mandating exclusion of pelvic or nodal tumour
reference.prognosis: Primary lymphoedema is a chronic, incurable condition that tends to progress without treatment, but structured decongestive therapy and infection prevention allow most patients to maintain limb function and quality of life. Prognosis worsens with recurrent cellulitis, advanced fibrosis and the rare development of angiosarcoma.
pitfalls: attributing chronic limb swelling to venous disease or simple obesity and missing lymphatic failure
undertreating or delaying antibiotics in cellulitis, allowing further lymphatic damage
overlooking associated syndromic features such as distichiasis, yellow nails or ptosis
failing to elicit a family history and thereby missing a hereditary diagnosis
dismissing new cutaneous lesions on a chronically swollen limb as bruising
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease
International Society of Lymphology Consensus Document on the diagnosis and treatment of peripheral lymphoedema
management: Complete decongestive therapy combining manual lymphatic drainage, multilayer compression bandaging and maintenance compression garments as the mainstay
Meticulous skin hygiene with emollients to maintain barrier integrity and reduce infection risk
Structured exercise, limb elevation and weight optimisation to support lymphatic drainage
Prompt antibiotic treatment of cellulitis and prophylactic antibiotics for recurrent episodes, since each attack accelerates lymphatic destruction
Surgical options in selected cases, including lymphaticovenous anastomosis, vascularised lymph node transfer, and liposuction or debulking for advanced fibrotic disease
Ongoing monitoring of limb volume and function with lymphoedema-specialist follow-up and psychological support
Genetic counselling and family screening for Mendelian forms such as Milroy disease and lymphoedema-distichiasis
